title: Find the Most Competitive Subsequence
description: Find the lexicographically smallest length-k subsequence, using a monotonic increasing stack with a remaining-elements budget check.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and a positive integer k, return the most competitive subsequence of nums of length k. Subsequence a is more competitive than subsequence b of the same length if, at the first index where they differ, a has the smaller value.

blocks.caption: A monotonic increasing stack, sized down to at most k, pops a worse recent choice when a strictly better one arrives and enough elements remain to still fill the target length.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums[] (order must be preserved, it is a subsequence), k (target length)"],["Competitiveness rule","Lexicographically smaller at the first differing position wins"],["Output","The single most competitive length-k subsequence"]]}

blocks.text: "Most competitive" (lexicographically smallest) subsequence of a fixed length is a classic monotonic stack problem: greedily prefer smaller values early, but only discard a previously chosen larger value if there are still enough REMAINING elements in the array to reach the target length k after discarding it.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: The same "greedy monotonic stack with a remaining-elements budget check" idea as Remove K Digits, just building UP to exactly k elements instead of removing down to a target count.

Picture assembling a lineup of exactly k contestants, one at a time, in the order they appear. Whenever a new contestant would clearly beat the current LAST person in the lineup, that weaker last person should be swapped out, but only if there are still enough contestants left to come to still fill the lineup back up to k after the swap.

blocks.caption: A weaker recent pick is replaced only if enough contestants remain to still reach size k.

items: A monotonic increasing stack (smallest values kept toward the bottom whenever possible) naturally builds the lexicographically smallest sequence.

The pop condition needs a "budget check": popping is only allowed if (current stack size - 1) + (remaining elements including the current one) is still at least k, otherwise popping would make it impossible to ever reach length k.
Once the stack has size k, no more pushes happen, since only exactly k elements are needed.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The final stack is [2, 3, 3, 4], matching the expected output. At i=6 and i=7, no popping happens even though 9 and 6 are irrelevant since they are larger than the stack top, and no room remains to push them anyway.
A brute-force approach could enumerate every possible length-k subsequence and compare them lexicographically, which is combinatorially infeasible for anything but tiny arrays.

The greedy monotonic-stack insight: to make the sequence lexicographically smallest, prefer a smaller value as early as possible, popping a larger recent choice whenever a smaller one arrives, AS LONG AS there are still enough elements remaining (including the current one) to eventually fill the stack back up to size k. This budget check is exactly what prevents over-popping.
Enumerate every combination of k indices (preserving order), and keep the lexicographically smallest resulting subsequence.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(C(n, k) * k)","Enumerates every length-k combination, each compared in O(k)"],["Space","O(k)","The current combination and best-so-far"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: The number of combinations grows combinatorially, making this infeasible for n up to 10^5 as in the actual constraints.

Use a monotonic increasing stack, capped at size k. For each number, pop the stack top while it is larger than the current number AND enough elements remain (stack size after popping, plus remaining array elements including the current one, is still at least k). Push the current number if the stack has fewer than k elements.

items: Iterate nums once, maintaining a stack.
Pop condition: stack not empty, top > current, and (stack.size() - 1 + remaining count) >= k.

items: A "lexicographically smallest subsequence of fixed length" problem is a monotonic stack with a remaining-elements budget check on the pop condition.
The budget check, (stack size - 1) + remaining elements >= k, is what prevents greedily popping too aggressively and running out of elements to reach the target length.
This is the mirror image of Remove K Digits, which builds down to n-k elements instead of up to exactly k.

blocks.text: Find the Most Competitive Subsequence is solved with a monotonic increasing stack capped at size k, greedily popping a larger recent choice for a smaller new value whenever enough elements remain to still reach length k. This budget-checked greedy approach finds the lexicographically smallest length-k subsequence in a single O(n) pass.
